name: Manscaped trimmers

card.summary: Heavily marketed men's body-grooming trimmer brand; criticised for premium pricing.
card.note: Reviews cited by Grokipedia raise pricing and trim-guard durability concerns.

quick.overview:
Manscaped sells electric trimmers aimed at male body and pubic grooming, with a strongly humorous direct-to-consumer brand.

Trimming is cosmetic and temporary; no clinical studies were found.
quick.mechanism: Rotary or foil blades cut hair at skin level, with guards for length.
quick.risks: Nicks or irritation are generally possible; critics cite price and guard durability.

lead: Manscaped is a San Diego direct-to-consumer grooming brand whose best-known product is the Lawn Mower, an electric trimmer made for body and pubic hair. People use it to keep body hair short and neat, which is part of the grooming approach known as manscaping: the term combines "man" and "landscaping" and refers to men trimming or removing body hair for aesthetic or sexual reasons.[1][2][3]

The company was founded in 2016 by Steve King and Paul Tran and built its brand on humour-driven advertising, puns and celebrity appearances.[1] Its range also includes the Weed Whacker nose and ear trimmer, the Crop Shaver and the Beard Hedger for facial hair, plus hygiene products sold direct and through retailers.[1][4]

Manscaped's trimmers use a rounded-blade design marketed as SkinSafe, with guards intended to reduce nicks and snags, waterproof construction rated IPX7 and rechargeable batteries, according to Grokipedia's description of the line.[4] Critics, as summarised there, have questioned the premium price and the durability of the adjustable guards.[4]

chain: Electric trimmer with guard shortens body hair evenly
angle.text: The trimmer lets men shorten body and pubic hair to a uniform length without fully shaving it, a look described in manscaping coverage as aesthetic grooming. Because the effect lasts only until the hair regrows, users repeat the trim periodically.

paras: Grokipedia describes the Lawn Mower 4.0 Pro as having replaceable blades, an LED light and a wireless-charging option, and the 5.0 Ultra as adding swappable foil and trimmer heads, a constant-speed motor meant to prevent pulling and adjustable temperature-based lighting. Both are listed with adjustable combs from 2 to 12 mm.[4] The Weed Whacker 3.0 Pro uses a rotary dual-blade system for nose and ear hair, and most trimmers in the range are described as waterproof with around 60 minutes of battery life and a travel lock.[4]
Products are sold through the brand's own site and through retailers such as Amazon, Target and Best Buy, with the Peak Hygiene Plan as a subscription option.[4]

Manscaped LLC was founded in 2016 by Steve King and Paul Tran; King was the original CEO and Tran later became CEO.[1] In October 2018, Steve King and Josh King pitched on ABC's Shark Tank seeking $500,000, and Mark Cuban and Lori Greiner made a handshake offer for a 25 percent stake that Cuban later said never materialised.[1]

A late-2020 campaign featured NFL player Rob Gronkowski and model Camille Kostek.[1] In July 2021 the company was reported in merger talks with the special-purpose acquisition company Bright Lights, and in November 2021 the merger was confirmed at a valuation of around $1 billion. The companies later cancelled it, with the cited announcement dated August 2022 and attributed to unfavourable market conditions.[1]

The Wikipedia article on manscaping says body-hair grooming dates back to ancient Egypt and Greece, that athletes have trimmed or removed body hair for a possible competitive edge in sports such as wrestling, running, swimming and cycling, and that aesthetic and sexual grooming has revived in recent decades.[2] It lists motivations including making a favourable first impression, competitiveness in tight job markets and sexual or aesthetic preference.[2] It dates the term's first known use to 2003.[2]

Grokipedia reports that critics argue the premium price reflects masculine branding more than performance, calling it a "gun metal gray tax", that some users report adjustable trim guards on the Lawn Mower 5.0 detaching in use, and that some commentators say the brand's marketing plays on grooming insecurities.[4]

It also lists legal disputes: a 2019 suit by Wahl Clipper over trademark and trade-practice claims, a 2024 declaratory-judgment action by Manspot over product naming, and a 2025 patent suit by Skull Shaver that was dismissed.[4]
